corrected_value.title: Which fearful toddlers should we worry about? Context, fear regulation, and anxiety risk.

decisions.quote: The goals of the present study included (1) replication of identifying a pattern of dysregulated fear in toddlers (Buss, 2011) in a new sample; (2) replication of the prediction from toddler dysregulated fear to elevated social inhibition (Buss, 2011; Buss et al., 2013); and (3) extending our understanding of the implications of dysregulated fear for children’s development by linking this pattern of high fearfulness in low-threat contexts to physiological reactivity as a putative psychophysiological marker of dysregulated emotion processes in toddlerhood.

decisions.quote: The goals of the present study included (1) replication of identifying a pattern of dysregulated fear in toddlers (Buss, 2011) in a new sample; (2) replication of the prediction from toddler dysregulated fear to elevated social inhibition (Buss, 2011; Buss et al., 2013); and (3) extending our understanding of the implications of dysregulated fear for children’s development by linking this pattern of high fearfulness in low-threat contexts to physiological reactivity as a putative psychophysiological marker of dysregulated emotion processes in toddlerhood. Results were largely consistent with expectations—we were able to replicate the identification of children with dysregulated fear in this new sample, showed that this pattern of fear responding predicted inhibition across early childhood, and identified modest evidence for the idea that children who manifest a dysregulated fear pattern of behavior would also show a distinct pattern of physiological responding to laboratory challenges.
decisions.reason: With row 418 resolved to Buss (2011), the authors explicitly conclude that they replicated both the identification of dysregulated fear in toddlers and its longitudinal association with elevated social inhibition.

raw_expert_opinion.quote: Tracked for four years, dysregulated fear was associated with greater social withdrawal (Buss, 2011) throughout the preschool years and kindergarten, as well as social anxiety disorder symptoms (Buss et al., 2013) at 6 years, compared to a more normative fear profile.
raw_expert_opinion.reason: In the prior adjudication for c931e17eb50f6ca0, shipped input_row_index 418 was corrected to Buss (2011) (doi:10.1037/a0023227, blind target 0), while target 1 (Buss et al., 2013) was marked blind_right with an invalid schema payload. Independent source review shows that Buss (2011) and Buss et al. (2013) are same-study follow-up waves of the exact same original cohort of N = 111 toddlers ('Tracked for four years, dysregulated fear was associated with greater social withdrawal (Buss, 2011) throughout the preschool years and kindergarten, as well as social anxiety disorder symptoms (Buss et al., 2013) at 6 years'; referred to in the singular throughout as 'a low risk, community sample', 'In the original sample', 'In the previous cohort', and contrasted with the present study's 'second cohort of children', lines 90-95, 464-465, 475). Furthermore, the present study only followed its second cohort from 24 to 48 months (preschool: ages 2, 3, and 4 years) and tested only (1) identification of the 24-month dysregulated fear pattern (Buss, 2011) and (2) its longitudinal association with parent-reported social inhibition across preschool at 24, 36, and 48 months (already reported for the original cohort in Buss, 2011), without following children to kindergarten (age 6) or assessing social anxiety disorder symptoms ('to date we have only followed these children into early childhood', line 472). Because target 1 is a same-cohort follow-up citation whose retested preschool social-inhibition finding is already represented by Buss (2011) (target 0 / corrected row 418), retaining a second row would duplicate the same original study and retested finding.
